1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5.name: Bishop's Opening: Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5.background: Black's symmetrical reply, also called the Boi Variation, and after 2...Nf6 and 2...Nc6 the next most common answer to 2.Bc4.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3.strategy: Prepares d4, which would give White a broad pawn centre with tempo on the bishop. The price is that the pawn takes the c3 square from the queen's knight and White is slow to develop, so the game stays quiet and strategic unless Black reacts to the threatened centre at once.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3.name: Bishop's Opening: Philidor Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to drag the bishop off its diagonal: if Black takes, c3 hits it with tempo and White gets a broad pawn centre for the pawn. It is the Evans Gambit idea played before the king's knight is out, so White gambles on time and the centre, not on material.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4.name: Bishop's Opening: McDonnell Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.d4.strategy: Challenges the bishop and the centre at once by offering the d-pawn. Black can take it with the e-pawn or the bishop, because the bishop guards d4 and the queen cannot recapture there, so White has to play for open lines and development against an extra pawn.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.d4.name: Bishop's Opening: Lewis Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2.strategy: Defends e4 and f2 with the queen, but it takes the e2 square from the bishop and does nothing against Black's symmetrical set-up, so Black develops without difficulty. A quiet, harmless move.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2.name: Bishop's Opening: Lopez Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.f4.strategy: Strikes at e5 as in the King's Gambit, but with the bishop on c5 the picture changes: the f-pawn no longer shields the king's diagonal, so Black's queen can check on h4 and the bishop eyes the knight on g1. A break with no developed pieces behind it.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.f4.name: Bishop's Opening: Stein Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4.strategy: Accepts the gambit: Black wins a pawn, but the bishop will be hit again by c3 and spend time on the move. The extra pawn is kept by developing calmly and not letting White's centre and open lines grow unchallenged.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4 at once, and lets White build the pawn centre it wants. Black does not stop the centre but counts on hitting it with pieces and a well-timed central break, which leads to the main line of this variation and to lively open play.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5.strategy: Meets the threatened centre by striking in the centre first: the pawn hits the bishop on c4 and opens lines for Black's pieces. If White takes the pawn, Black plays for quick development and activity instead of material, so this is the sharp, energetic answer.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Qg5.strategy: Brings the queen out early to hit g2, but it ignores the centre: White can strike with d4 and attack the bishop at once. Black spends time on a raid while the other pieces stay at home.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Qg5.name: Bishop's Opening: del Rio Variation

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6.strategy: Develops and defends e5 in one move, the solid reply to the quiet queen move. Black keeps the symmetrical structure and stays flexible, with no weaknesses and an easy game, while White's queen has still to find a useful task.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, so the queen on e2 has to do the defending. Black gets a more active game than with the quiet defence of e5, and the queen is tied to the defence of the pawn on e4 for now.
